cards.question: A loop has a battery and three bulbs in series. Where is the current smallest?
options: Nowhere: it's the same all the way round
cards.why: In a single loop the current is the same at every point, while the bulbs convert electrical energy into light and heat.

cards.question: Why does a lamp light the instant you close the switch, though electrons drift less than a millimetre a second?
options: The wire is already full of charge, and the push travels almost at the speed of light
The battery fires electrons down the wire very fast
The lamp stores charge from last time
cards.why: Every electron in the loop starts drifting at once, because the push travels round the whole loop almost instantly.

cards.question: What does "5 V at this point" mean on a schematic?
cards.why: Voltage is always a difference between two points; a voltage stated at a single point is measured relative to ground.

cards.question: Your meter is in amps mode and you touch the probes across a lamp. What happens?
options: It shorts the lamp out and probably blows the meter's fuse
cards.why: In amps mode a meter has very low resistance, nearly like a plain wire, so it must be placed in series inside a break in the loop.

cards.question: You need 12 V to push 25 mA through a resistor. Which do you fit?
cards.why: R = V / I = 12 / 0.025 = 480 Ω, and 470 Ω is the nearest standard E12 value.

cards.question: Why do filament bulbs usually fail just as they're switched on?
options: A cold filament has low resistance, so it takes a surge of current
The voltage is higher at switch-on
cards.why: Cold tungsten has about a tenth of its hot resistance, so at switch-on the filament draws a brief surge of current several times normal.

cards.question: What do two parts in parallel always share?
cards.why: Both their ends are joined, so they have the same voltage across them. The current splits between them.

cards.question: What do two parts in series always share?
cards.why: There's only one path, so the same current goes through both. The voltage splits between them.

cards.question: Three wires meet. 40 mA flows in on one and 15 mA out on another. What flows on the third?
cards.why: All current flowing into a junction flows out: 40 mA enters, so 40 mA leaves in total, and 40 - 15 = 25 mA goes out on the third wire.

cards.question: You put a 10 kΩ resistor in parallel with a 1 kΩ resistor. The combined resistance of the pair is...
cards.why: Each parallel path adds another way for current to flow, so the combined resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor: about 909 Ω.

cards.question: Why not put a fresh battery in parallel with a flat one?
options: Current flows from the fresh one into the flat one
The voltages add and overload the circuit
cards.why: The fresh battery pushes current back into the flat one, wasting charge and warming both. Big batteries can do it hard enough to be dangerous.

cards.question: A string of parts has stopped working. Across which part will you read the full supply voltage?
options: The one with the break in it
cards.why: With no current, nothing else drops any voltage, so all of it appears across the break.

cards.question: Two equal resistors in series across 9 V. What's at the point between them, unloaded?
cards.why: Equal resistors share the voltage equally. Out = 9 x R / (R + R) = 4.5 V.

cards.question: Why does a divider's output fall when you connect a load?
options: The load in parallel makes the bottom resistance smaller
cards.why: Two resistances in parallel are less than either, so the bottom's share of the voltage shrinks.

cards.question: What does a stiffer divider cost you?
options: More current, wasted all the time
cards.why: Lower resistances carry more current, whether the load is there or not.

cards.question: A source reads 12 V open and 11 V while delivering 0.5 A. What's its inside resistance?
cards.why: It lost 1 V inside at 0.5 A: 1 / 0.5 = 2 Ω.

cards.question: To keep a signal's voltage, feed it into...
cards.why: A high input impedance pulls little current, so the source hardly sags.

cards.question: Measured open, shorted and loaded, a solar panel's points...
options: bend: it holds its voltage, then collapses
cards.why: Inside a solar panel, light generates a steady current in parallel with the silicon cell's built-in diode, so the voltage stays nearly flat until the load draws almost all the available current.

cards.question: Three times the current through a resistor means how much heat?
cards.why: Power is P = I^2 x R, so tripling the current multiplies the heat by 3^2 = 9.

cards.question: A 24 V, 100 Ah battery holds...
cards.why: Watt-hours equal volts times amp-hours: 24 V x 100 Ah = 2400 Wh, or 2.4 kWh.

cards.question: Why do larger off-grid systems run at 48 V rather than 12 V?
options: A quarter of the current, so a sixteenth of the cable loss
cards.why: Delivering the same power at four times the voltage requires a quarter of the current, so I^2 x R cable heating falls to one sixteenth.

cards.question: What does a fuse protect?
cards.why: The fuse must melt before the cable insulation overheats, so it is rated above the load's running current and at or below the cable's ampacity.

cards.question: A load matched to its source's inside resistance gets the most power. What's the catch?
options: Half the energy is wasted inside the source
cards.why: When load resistance equals source internal resistance, the source and load dissipate equal power (50% efficiency). Power systems keep source resistance much smaller than load resistance so nearly all the energy reaches the load.

cards.question: How do you find a high-resistance joint?
options: Measure the voltage across it with the current flowing
Measure its resistance with the power off
cards.why: Under load, a resistive joint drops voltage that you can read directly with a voltmeter. With the circuit off, no current flows to create a voltage drop, and a multimeter's tiny resistance-mode test current often fails to reveal a faulty power connection.

cards.question: A wave repeats every 10 ms. Its frequency is...
cards.why: Frequency is one divided by the period: 1 / 0.01 s = 100 Hz.

cards.question: A signal swings 0.4 V each way around its middle. Its peak to peak is...
cards.why: Peak-to-peak voltage from bottom to top is twice the amplitude.

cards.question: A stage on 12 V can swing from 1 V to 11 V. Where should its steady voltage sit?
cards.why: Sitting halfway between the limits gives the same headroom up and down.

cards.question: The bottoms of a wave come out flat, the tops don't. The steady voltage is...
cards.why: The wave runs into the bottom limit first, so it sits too close to it. Raising the steady voltage gives the bottom half more room.

cards.question: A guitar note at 110 Hz also has quieter sines at...
cards.why: Harmonics are at whole multiples of the note; their mix is the instrument's tone.

cards.question: A pedal passes no sound. Its buffer's input should sit at 4.5 V and reads 9 V. Most likely...
options: the resistor pulling it down is open
cards.why: The input has gone to the top: whatever should pull it down to the middle isn't working. A flat battery would make it lower than 4.5 V, not 9 V.

cards.question: 10 kΩ and 100 µF have a time constant of...
A capacitor charges with τ = 2 s. When is it nearly full?
cards.why: A capacitor reaches over 99% of its final voltage in about five time constants (10 s here). After one time constant (2 s), it is only 63% of the way.

cards.question: In a circuit that has settled, how much current flows through a capacitor?
options: The same as through the resistor before it
cards.why: Once the capacitor has charged to the steady DC voltage, no more DC current flows; only changing voltages push charge back and forth.

cards.question: R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF in a low-pass filter. The corner is about...
cards.why: f = 1 / (2π x 1000 Ω x 0.0000001 F), which is about 1592 Hz.

cards.question: Turning a tone knob that raises R in a low-pass filter makes the sound...
cards.why: A bigger R lowers the corner, so more of the highs are cut.

cards.question: You switch off a relay coil. Across the opening switch there is, for an instant...
options: a spike far above the supply voltage
cards.why: The collapsing magnetic field keeps current moving and drives the voltage as high as needed to cross the opening gap until the stored energy is spent.

cards.question: A conducting silicon diode drops about...
cards.why: Past its knee, a silicon diode holds about 0.6 to 0.7 V whatever the current.

cards.question: A red LED (2 V) on 12 V at 10 mA needs a resistor of about...
Why can't you run an LED straight from a 3 V battery that "matches" its voltage?
options: A little extra voltage makes a lot of current, so nothing sets it
cards.why: Past the knee the current climbs steeply with tiny voltage changes, so a series resistor is needed to set the current.

cards.question: Warm a silicon diode by 50 °C. Its forward voltage...
cards.why: A silicon diode's forward voltage drops by about 2 mV for every degree Celsius it warms.

cards.question: A 50 Hz half-wave rectifier feeds 10 mA from 1000 µF. The ripple is about...
Which clipping diodes let the most signal through before they clip?
cards.why: LEDs have the highest knee, near 2 V, so they clip later and louder.

cards.question: With β = 150 and 0.2 mA into the base, the collector can carry up to...
cards.why: The maximum collector current in the active region is β x base current = 150 x 0.2 mA = 30 mA.

cards.question: To drive 5 mA into a transistor base from a 5 V pin, the base resistor should be about...
cards.why: Subtracting the 0.7 V base-emitter drop leaves 4.3 V across the resistor, and (5 - 0.7) / 0.005 A = 860 Ω.

cards.question: Why is a transistor switch that is only half on a problem?
options: It drops volts at full current, and heats
It draws too much base current
cards.why: Power dissipated in the transistor equals the collector-emitter voltage times the collector current, and both are substantial when the switch is half on.

cards.question: A MOSFET's gate voltage is 0.5 V above its threshold. It is...
cards.why: The threshold is only the voltage where the MOSFET begins to conduct; it needs several volts above threshold to reach its low on-resistance.

cards.question: Without a flyback diode, switching a relay coil off can...
options: kill the transistor with a voltage spike
cards.why: The coil's inductance keeps current flowing when the switch opens, driving the collector voltage far past the transistor's breakdown rating.

cards.question: A load stays on with the control off, and the transistor's base reads 0 V. Most likely...
cards.why: With 0 V from base to emitter the transistor should be cut off, so current flowing from collector to emitter means the transistor has failed shorted.

cards.question: Rc = 6.8 kΩ, Re = 680 Ω. The gain is about...
cards.why: The voltage gain is about Rc / Re = 6800 / 680 = 10.

cards.question: A common-emitter stage's output, compared with its input, is...
cards.why: A rising base voltage causes more current to flow through Rc, which drops more voltage across Rc and pulls the collector voltage down.

cards.question: An amplifier on 12 V clips its bottoms early. Its collector probably sits...
cards.why: When the collector is biased too low, the downward swing hits saturation before the upward swing reaches the positive supply.

cards.question: Why put an emitter follower after a guitar pickup?
options: So a heavy load doesn't pull the pickup's signal down
cards.why: Its high input impedance keeps the pickup from being loaded down, and its low output impedance easily drives the next stage or cable.

cards.question: For a gain of 21 in a non-inverting op-amp stage with Rg = 1 kΩ, Rf should be...
cards.why: The gain is 1 + Rf / Rg = 21, so Rf / Rg = 20 and Rf = 20 kΩ.

cards.question: In a Tube Screamer the clipping diodes sit...
options: in the op-amp's feedback, across Rf
cards.why: Putting the diodes across Rf lowers the feedback resistance once the signal exceeds a diode drop, rounding off the peaks smoothly.

cards.question: How do you find a schematic's Q1 on its board?
options: By the silkscreen label beside it
By its position on the schematic
cards.why: The board's layout differs from the drawing; the printed names match.

cards.question: The first step in fault-finding a dead circuit is...
options: Work out what each point should read
Replace the parts most likely to fail
cards.why: Measurements only mean something against what they should be.

cards.question: 9 V across a stretch of copper trace means...
cards.why: Intact copper has negligible resistance and drops almost 0 V, whereas a break acts as an open circuit with the full supply voltage across it.

cards.question: A dry solder joint usually looks...
options: Dull and grainy, or balled up
cards.why: Good solder wets the lead and pad to flow into a neat, concave cone, whereas a dry joint fails to wet the metal and stays rough or balled up.

cards.question: With a hundred possible fault points in a chain, half-splitting takes about...
cards.why: 2^7 = 128, so seven halvings cover a hundred points.
